# Error Budgets & Prioritization: SLOs, Customer Impact, Resource Allocation ## First Principles: SLO, SLI, and Error Budget **SLO (Service Level Objective):** A target. "We promise 99.9% uptime." **SLI (Service Level Indicator):** A measurement. "We achieved 99.87% uptime this month." **Error budget:** The difference. If you promised 99.9% and achieved 99.87%, you spent 0.03% of your budget and have 0% left for the month. ``` SLO: 99.9% uptime (0.1% = 8.76 hours/month downtime allowed) SLI: 99.87% actual (0.13% = 9.36 hours/month downtime) Error budget: spent 0.03% / 0.1% = 30% of budget Interpretation: - You've used 30% of error budget - You have 70% left (6 hours) for rest of month - If you deploy a risky change and it fails for 1 hour, you've spent another 3% of budget - Question: Can you afford that risk now? Or should you wait for next month? ``` **Why this matters:** ``` Without error budget thinking: - Team deploys risky feature Friday afternoon - Feature causes 20 min outage Saturday 2 AM - Customers are angry - CEO asks: "Why did you deploy Friday?" - Answer: "We didn't know it would break" With error budget thinking: - Friday morning: Check error budget (70% remaining) - Feature risk: Medium (could cause 5% outage) - Decision: Wait until Monday morning (fresh week = fresh budget) - Monday 10 AM: Deploy, monitor closely - If outage occurs, happens during business hours when team can respond ``` --- ## The Problem: Unlimited Bugs, Limited Time You're a staff engineer at a $1B SaaS company. Your team has: - 50 feature requests in backlog - 30 bugs reported (10 blocking customers, 20 minor) - 15 technical debt items (slow deploys, flaky tests, old dependencies) - 3 engineers, 6-week sprint **Impossible to do all of it. How do you prioritize?** ``` Without error budget thinking: - Build features (customer-facing revenue) - Fix critical bugs (immediate pain) - Ignore tech debt (can fix later) → Deploys slow down, tests become flaky, incidents increase → Next quarter: 50% of time fighting fires instead of building With error budget thinking: - Calculate: If we do X, can we stay within SLO? - If yes: do it - If no: fix operational issues first → Predictable velocity, fewer incidents ``` --- ## Deriving Prioritization From Error Budget **Framework:** ```mermaid graph TD A["Current SLI

You have 6 weeks. **Current state:** ``` SLO: 99.9% (8.76 hours/month downtime) SLI so far this month: 99.95% (4.38 hours downtime used) Error budget remaining: ~4 hours (45% of budget) Incidents last month: - 2 outages (main database, 2 hours total) - 5 degradations (slow API, 1 hour total) - Root causes: buggy feature flag, missing index, memory leak Backlog: 1. Feature A: $500K/quarter if launched (3 weeks, medium risk) 2. Bug: Memory leak (3 days, low risk, prevents incidents) 3. Feature B: $100K/quarter if launched (2 weeks, high risk) 4. Flaky tests slowing deploys (1 week, low risk) 5. Database index missing (2 days, low risk) ``` **Prioritization decision (with error budget):** ``` Week 1–2: Reduce risk (because budget is tight) - Fix memory leak (3 days) - Add missing database index (2 days) - Fix flaky tests (5 days) → Goal: No incidents for 2 weeks, restore confidence Week 3–4: Feature A (medium risk, high value) - 3 weeks of development - Deploy with feature flag (low risk because flag lets us revert instantly) - After 1 week, we have 3 hours error budget left (enough to handle incidents) Week 5–6: Start Feature B (high value, but risky) - 2 weeks of development - Do NOT deploy yet (finish after error budget resets next month) - Deploy first week of next month when budget is fresh Rationale: - We spent 50% of error budget fixing bugs - This prevents future incidents (expected: save 2–3 hours/month) - Feature A is deployed with safety (feature flag) - Feature B waits for next month (too risky to launch when budget is low) ``` --- ## SLI Definition Matters How you define SLI determines what you optimize for: ``` Option 1: "99.9% of requests succeed" Measures: Did the request return a 2xx status code? Problem: Slow request (5 second latency) is still a "success" Consequence: Team doesn't care about performance (counts as success) Option 2: "99.9% of requests return within 1 second" Measures: Latency percentile (P99.9 < 1 second) Problem: 1 second might be too strict for batch jobs Consequence: Team optimizes latency, but overbuilds for some workloads Option 3: "99.9% of user-facing requests return within 1 second" Measures: Latency for requests from logged-in users (exclude background jobs) Problem: Might ignore batch job reliability Consequence: Balanced: users get fast responses, batch jobs can be slower BEST PRACTICE: - Define SLI that matches customer experience - Segment by customer type (premium vs free, user vs batch) - Review quarterly (is this still the right goal?) ``` --- ## Story Card: Feature Launch During Low Error Budget **Scenario:** It's end of month. Error budget is nearly empty. **Team wants to ship Feature X (risky database migration) Friday afternoon before holiday.** ``` Friday 9 AM: Staff engineer reviews Error budget: <0.5% remaining (15 minutes downtime available) Feature risk: Medium (could cause 1–2% outage if buggy) Holiday: Monday–Wednesday (no team on call) Decision: DO NOT DEPLOY FRIDAY Reasons: 1. If bug happens Friday 5 PM, team is gone for 3 days 2. Error budget is empty (can't afford any incidents) 3. Even if feature is good, we don't have margin for error Alternative: Deploy Monday at 10 AM 1. Team is on call, can respond instantly to issues 2. Error budget resets (new month = new budget) 3. Feature still ships this month, but safely Team reaction: "But we wanted to ship before holiday!" Staff engineer: "You will. Monday instead of Friday. Better to ship safely." Result: - Feature launched Monday with zero incidents - If we'd launched Friday, 1-hour outage Saturday → customer impact, post-mortem ``` **Key insight:** Error budget helps you say "no" to risky timing, even when pressure is high. --- ## Allocating Time: Feature vs Operational Work Use error budget to decide feature velocity: ``` Low error budget month (< 10% remaining): Allocation: - 60% reducing technical debt / fixing bugs - 20% fighting incidents (reactive) - 20% new features Why: We're unstable. Stabilize first. Mid error budget month (10–50% remaining): Allocation: - 40% reducing technical debt / operational work - 10% incident response - 50% new features Why: We can take calculated risks while improving stability. High error budget month (> 50% remaining): Allocation: - 20% operational work - 5% incident response - 75% new features Why: System is stable. Go fast. ``` --- ## When to Use / When NOT to Use Error Budget Framework | Scenario | Use Error Budget? | Example | |----------|------------------|---------| | SaaS product (customer-facing) | YES | Stripe, Notion, GitHub | | Internal tool | MAYBE | If used by critical path, yes; if not, just fix bugs when found | | Startup MVP | NO | Stability is secondary; ship fast | | Infrastructure (platform) | YES | Kubernetes, database cluster | | Open-source library | MAYBE | If widely used, yes; if niche, not critical | | One-time batch job | NO | Success or failure is binary, not about uptime | | Real-time trading system | YES | Error budget is hours/year, not hours/month | --- ## Reasoning Framework: Incident Response Using Error Budget ``` Incident occurs: "API is 10x slower than normal" Step 1: Measure impact - What % of requests are affected? (100% of user API) - Latency: was 100ms, now 1 second (10x) - Duration: how long will it last? (15 min estimated) Step 2: Calculate error budget cost - 100% of traffic × 15 minutes = 100% * 15/(30*24*60) ≈ 0.035% (month) - How much budget do we have? (say, 5% remaining) - Decision: We can afford the 15 min downtime. Continue debugging normally. Step 3: But if budget was < 1%? - Immediate decision: Rollback or kill feature (save error budget) - Root cause analysis happens after SLA is safe - This is OK. Different risk calculus when budget is low. ``` --- ## Q&A (Built on Fundamentals) **Recall 1:** Your SLO is 99.9% uptime. Your SLI this month is 99.85%. How much error budget do you have left? *Must-say:* - 99.9% SLO = 0.1% error budget = 8.76 hours/month - 99.85% SLI = 0.15% used = 12.96 hours spent - Wait, that's over budget. How did that happen? *Correct interpretation:* - If you achieved 99.85%, you've USED 50% of budget and have 50% left - Or you're over SLA (which is a problem—need incident review) **Probe 1:** Your team is pushing to launch Feature A on Friday. Feature is risky (could cause outage). Your error budget is 1% remaining. What do you say? *Expected:* - "No. Too risky. Wait until Monday." - Reasons: (1) budget is tight, (2) team won't be on call Friday evening, (3) holiday weekend = slow response - You're being a staff engineer: protecting both feature velocity AND stability **Probe 2:** You have two projects: Feature B (safe, medium value) and Refactor C (risky, high operational benefit). Which do you do first? *Expected:* - Depends on error budget - Low budget: Refactor C first (reduce future incidents, make velocity stable) - High budget: Feature B first (safe, ships revenue) - Staff engineer's job: explain the trade-off **Numeric 1:** Your SLO is 99% uptime. You have 30 days in the month. How many hours can you be down? *Working:* - 99% = 1% error budget - 1 month = 30 * 24 = 720 hours - 1% * 720 = 7.2 hours - You can afford 7 hours 12 minutes of downtime this month **Numeric 2:** You've used 6 hours of your 7.2-hour budget. You want to deploy a feature that's 95% confident (5% chance of 1-hour outage). Can you deploy? *Working:* - Error budget remaining: 7.2 - 6 = 1.2 hours - Feature risk: 5% * 1 hour = 0.05 hours expected outage - But worst case: 5% chance of 1 hour outage = risk is too high - Decision: NO, don't deploy. Wait for next month. - Alternative: Deploy with feature flag (can revert in 5 minutes if bad) --- ## Questions for the Interviewer - How does your team use error budgets? - Have you had to say "no" to a feature launch based on SLO risk? - How do you define SLI for your system? - How do you balance feature velocity with reliability? - What happens when you run out of error budget mid-month? --- ## Checklist: Error Budget Governance - [ ] **1. SLO is written and agreed:** Not vague ("stable"), specific ("99.9% uptime") - ❌ Wrong: SLO is assumed, not documented - ✓ Right: "SLO: 99.9% uptime, P99 latency < 1 second, measured monthly" - [ ] **2. SLI measures what customers care about:** Not just "requests that don't error" - ❌ Wrong: "99.9% of requests return a status code" (includes 5xx errors as success) - ✓ Right: "99.9% of requests return 2xx with latency < 1 second" - [ ] **3. Error budget is tracked in real-time:** Team knows status at any point in month - ❌ Wrong: "We'll check SLO at end of month" - ✓ Right: Dashboard showing SLI, error budget %, and forecast for month - [ ] **4. Deployment risk is assessed against budget:** Risky changes don't launch when budget is tight - ❌ Wrong: Deploy whenever ready, regardless of error budget - ✓ Right: "Feature is 90% confident, budget is 2%, so wait for next month" - [ ] **5. Incidents are blameless, but tracked:** Post-mortem records how much error budget was spent and what failed - ❌ Wrong: "Who broke production?" (blame-focused, suppresses honesty) - ✓ Right: Post-mortem: "Root cause: missing index. Cost: 2 hours downtime = 20% of budget. Fix: add index, add monitoring."
